text: Dame Elisabeth Joy Murdoch, Lady Murdoch AC DBE (née Greene; 8 February 1909 – 5 December 2012), was an Australian philanthropist and matriarch of the Murdoch family. She married Sir Keith Murdoch in 1928, 23 years his junior, and inherited the bulk of his fortune upon his death in 1952. She was the mother of Rupert Murdoch, international media proprietor, and had other children: Janet Calvert-Jones AO (born 1939), Anne Kantor AO (1937–2022), and Helen Handbury AO (1929–2004). Born in Melbourne on 8 February 1909, she was the youngest of three daughters of Marie Grace de Lancey (née Forth) and Rupert Greene; her grandfather, William Henry Greene, was an Irish railway engineer who emigrated to Australia and married Fanny, the fourth of George Govett’s 10 daughters. Her mother’s ancestors were Scottish and English, with one maternal great-grandfather, Frederick Forth, serving as a lieutenant governor in the West Indies. She was educated at St Catherine's School in Toorak and Clyde School in Woodend. Before marriage, she volunteered with the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. She joined the management committee of the Royal Children's Hospital in 1933, serving as its president from 1954 to 1965, and was designated to succeed her predecessor Ella Latham; she oversaw the hospital’s relocation from Carlton to a new campus in Parkville. In 1961, she was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire, Civil Division (CBE) for her work at the hospital, and in 1963, a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire, Civil Division (DBE) for her role in building the new children's hospital. In 1989, she received a Companion of the Order of Australia, Civil Division (AC) for community services, and in 2001, the Centenary Medal for philanthropic contributions to the Australian arts. She was a Life Governor of the Royal Women's Hospital, patron of the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the Australian American Association (Victoria), a founding member of the EW Tipping Foundation and the Deafness Foundation of Victoria, and the first woman on the council of trustees of the National Gallery of Victoria. She was also a founding member of the Victorian Tapestry Workshop and a member of the Patrons Council of the Epilepsy Foundation of Victoria. Her garden, "Cruden Farm" at Langwarrin, designed by Edna Walling, is one of Australia’s finest landscape gardens and is open to the public. In 1983, she was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Laws by the University of Melbourne and became a fellow of Trinity College, Melbourne in 2000. A portrait of her by Christopher Pyett, adapted by Normana Wight and woven by Merrill Dumbrell, was commissioned for the National Portrait Gallery in 2000. In 2001, she was inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women and a rose, Treloars, was named after her. A Tasmanian Boronia species, Boronia elisabethiae, was named in her honour following donations to the Royal Botanic Gardens in Melbourne. In 2002, she received recognition from the French government for funding an Auguste Rodin exhibition in Melbourne. In 2003, she joined Philanthropy Australia as a life member and was awarded the key to the City of Melbourne. In 2004, Langwarrin Secondary College was renamed Elisabeth Murdoch College. In 2005, at age 96, she received the Victorian of the Year award. In 2009, the main performance venue of the Melbourne Recital Centre was named in her honour, and she was elected an Honorary Fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities. In 2010, Geelong Grammar School named a new girls' boarding house after her. In January 2007, at age 97 years and 11 months, she surpassed Dame Alice Chisholm as Australia’s longest-lived dame. She was also a patron of the Australian Family Association. She died in her sleep at Cruden Farm, Langwarrin, Victoria, on 5 December 2012, at the age of 103. At the time of her death, she had 77 living descendants.
